Education only. Not for diagnosis, treatment or any clinical decision.

## In 60 seconds

Every imaging test used around an EP procedure trades the same few things: how fine a detail it resolves, how
different two tissues look, how much noise sits on top, how much radiation or time it costs, and whether it can be
used in the lab at all. This module gives one vocabulary for all of them. Blur is a point-spread function with a
full width at half maximum; contrast and noise combine into a contrast-to-noise ratio; smoothing trades one for the
other. Published resolutions span more than an order of magnitude, from a 0.34-mm CT section [@rajendran2022] to
4–7 mm in clinical PET [@kinahan2010], and the left atrial wall is about 1.9 mm thick on average [@beinart2011], so
the same wall looks different in each. An imaging test's accuracy also depends on who is tested: CT for appendage
thrombus had 96% sensitivity and 92% specificity against TEE, but a pooled positive predictive value of 41% at 8.9%
prevalence [@romero2013]. The EACVI/EHRA consensus reviews echo, MRI, CT and nuclear imaging in AF [@donal2016];
modules m49–m55 take each modality in turn.

## From the field

- **Start from the question, not the scanner.** Where is the esophagus, is there thrombus, how thick is the wall,
  where is the scar, is there inflammation: each question has a modality that answers it best, and the table below
  gives one published example for each.
- **A resolution number is a blur, not a detection limit.** At routine LGE resolution the thinnest published atrial
  wall keeps about a third of its contrast (lab part B); whether it is "seen" then depends on noise and thresholds.
- **Contrast is chosen.** Blood and heart wall differ by about 5 HU in CT without contrast agent; iodine, gadolinium
  and tracers are how imaging separates them (lab part C).
- **Read the prevalence before the sensitivity.** The same CT protocol gives very different predictive values in a
  population where thrombus is rare and in one where it is common (@eq-m48-lr).

## Derivations

### Which modality answers which question

One published example per question. "Evidence" says what kind of study it is; each module goes further.

| Question | Modality | What one study found | Evidence | Module |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| How much radiation does a procedure give? | Fluoroscopy | Reference levels from 4.10 Gy·cm² (accessory pathway ablation) to 12.65 Gy·cm² (persistent AF ablation) across 33 centers [@greffier2026] | National survey | [m49](m49-fluoroscopy-radiation.qmd) |
| Can AF ablation be done without fluoroscopy? | Mapping system, ICE | Zero fluoroscopy feasible in 95.1% of 1,593 patients, with no significant difference in success or complications [@debreceni2023] | Meta-analysis of observational studies | [m49](m49-fluoroscopy-radiation.qmd), [m50](m50-intracardiac-echo.qmd) |
| ICE or TEE during AF ablation? | ICE, TEE | No significant difference in complications, shorter fluoroscopy with ICE; certainty low to very low [@kanniyan2026] | Meta-analysis, 6 studies | [m50](m50-intracardiac-echo.qmd) |
| Is there thrombus in the appendage? | CT, TEE | Sensitivity 96%, specificity 92%, pooled PPV 41% at 8.9% prevalence; with delayed imaging 100%, 99% and 92% [@romero2013] | Meta-analysis, TEE as reference | m48, [m51](m51-cardiac-ct.qmd) |
| Where is the esophagus? | CT | It touched the mid posterior left atrial wall in every patient [@tsao2005] | Cross-sectional CT study | [m51](m51-cardiac-ct.qmd) |
| How thick is the atrial wall? | CT | 1.89 mm on average, 0.5–3.5 mm [@beinart2011] | Observational CT study | [m51](m51-cardiac-ct.qmd) |
| How accurate is CT merged with the map? | CT and mapping | Reported registration error 2.3 mm with a surface fit against 6.4 mm with landmarks [@kistler2006] | Clinical series | [m51](m51-cardiac-ct.qmd), [m55](m55-multimodal-capstone.qmd) |
| Is "atrial fibrosis" a stable number? | MRI | Average burden from 5.0% to 37.4% of the wall depending on the threshold [@boyle2022] | Methods study | [m52](m52-cardiac-mri.qmd) |
| Where are the VT channels? | MRI | Conducting channels on MRI colocalized with functional mapping targets [@guichard2024] | Single-center cohort | [m52](m52-cardiac-mri.qmd) |
| Did the ablation leave gaps? | MRI | Scar gaps predicted the extent of vein reconnection but not its location [@aljefairi2019] | Prospective cohort | [m53](m53-lesion-imaging-interventional-mri.qmd) |
| Is there active inflammation? | FDG PET | In cardiac sarcoidosis with VT, no improvement on serial PET was associated with events [@muser2018] | Single-center cohort | [m54](m54-nuclear-imaging.qmd) |
| Is a device infected? | FDG PET/CT, SPECT | Multisociety consensus on uptake at device pockets and leads [@bourque2024] | Expert consensus | [m54](m54-nuclear-imaging.qmd) |

**Key takeaways**

- Each question has its own modality and its own evidence, from randomized trials to consensus.
- A finding belongs to its study's population, protocol and reference standard.

### Blur and resolution

Model a scanner's blur as a Gaussian point-spread function (PSF) $h$ of standard deviation $\sigma$. Its full width at
half maximum (FWHM) $\Gamma$ is the distance between the two points where it falls to half its peak. Two equal point
sources a distance $d$ apart, each blurred, show a dip between them only when the curvature of their sum at the
midpoint is positive:

$$
h(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\,e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}, \qquad \Gamma = 2\sqrt{2\ln 2}\;\sigma \approx 2.355\,\sigma,
\qquad \text{dip between two points} \iff d > 2\sigma \approx 0.85\,\Gamma
$$ {#eq-m48-psf}

Two points one FWHM apart show a dip of 7%; three standard deviations apart, 36% (lab part A). Published
resolutions, read as Gaussian FWHMs, span a wide range. A photon-counting CT system measured a thinnest section
(section-sensitivity FWHM) of 0.34 mm in its high-resolution mode and 0.64 mm in its standard mode, and reported
finer in-plane resolution still [@rajendran2022]. LGE MRI resolves about 1.5–2 mm routinely and about 1 mm when thin
walls are the target [@kellman2012]. Clinical PET resolves about 4–7 mm FWHM [@kinahan2010]. ICE resolves about
0.2 mm along the beam at 7.5 MHz with a short pulse, and less across it
([eq-m50-axial](m50-intracardiac-echo.qmd#eq-m50-axial)). Reading each as a Gaussian is a simplification: real PSFs
have other shapes, and an MRI voxel size is not exactly a FWHM.

**Key takeaways**

- FWHM ≈ 2.355 σ; two structures closer than about 0.85 FWHM merge.
- Across modalities, resolution differs by more than a factor of ten.

### Thin walls

A wall of thickness $w$ and unit contrast, blurred, peaks at $\operatorname{erf}(w/(2\sqrt2\,\sigma))$ of its
contrast ([eq-m51-wall](m51-cardiac-ct.qmd#eq-m51-wall), derived in m51). For the thinnest published left atrial
wall, 0.5 mm [@beinart2011], that is 92% at a 0.34-mm CT section, 44% at 1 mm, 31% at 1.5 mm and 12% at 4 mm. The
mean wall, 1.89 mm, keeps 86% at 1.5 mm and 42% at 4 mm (lab part B). Read with a fixed threshold at half the
contrast, the thin wall disappears once its peak falls below one half; read as the width at half of its own peak, it
never reads thinner than the blur.

::: {.demo #m48-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m48-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m48-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m48-d1-thin-walls.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: [eq-m51-wall](m51-cardiac-ct.qmd#eq-m51-wall), a uniform wall between two equal backgrounds, blurred by a
  1-D Gaussian; readings found by bisection. Tested against `epml.overview` and `epml.ct`.
- Presets: CT section FWHM [@rajendran2022], LGE resolution [@kellman2012], PET resolution [@kinahan2010], each read
  as a Gaussian FWHM. Wall thickness 0.5 and 1.89 mm marked [@beinart2011].
- What it ignores: noise, unequal backgrounds on the two sides (blood and fat), the true shape of each scanner's PSF,
  voxel sampling and motion.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- A wall thinner than the blur loses contrast before it loses width.
- Every thickness read from an image belongs with its resolution and its reading method.

### Contrast, noise and dose

Contrast is the difference between two tissues' signals; noise is the random scatter on each. Their ratio decides
what can be told apart:

$$
\mathrm{CNR} = \frac{|S_A - S_B|}{\sigma_n}, \qquad \mathrm{CNR}_n = \sqrt{n}\;\mathrm{CNR}_1
$$ {#eq-m48-cnr}

where $S_A$ and $S_B$ are mean signals, $\sigma_n$ is the noise standard deviation and $\mathrm{CNR}_n$ the value
after averaging $n$ independent samples. For photon-limited images the noise falls as one over the square root of
the counts, so halving it takes four times the dose ([eq-m49-cnr](m49-fluoroscopy-radiation.qmd#eq-m49-cnr)).
Contrast comes from physics and agents. With the 60-keV attenuation data of m49 and m51, wall and blood are 54 and
59 HU, and 2 mm of wall against blood changes an X-ray projection by 0.019%; 10 mg/mL of iodine (illustrative) lifts
blood to 427 HU. With the T1 values of Bauner et al. [@bauner2012], an infarct keeps 34% of the full signal when
normal myocardium is nulled (lab part C, m52).

Smoothing averages neighboring pixels. For white noise on a grid of spacing $\Delta$, a Gaussian smoothing kernel of
standard deviation $\sigma_s$ (much larger than $\Delta$) leaves

$$
\sigma_n' = \frac{\sigma_n\,\Delta}{2\sqrt{\pi}\,\sigma_s}, \qquad \sigma_{\text{tot}}^2 = \sigma^2 + \sigma_s^2
$$ {#eq-m48-smooth}

in two dimensions, while the blur grows to $\sigma_{\text{tot}}$. Putting blur and noise together, a wall of
contrast $C$ between equal backgrounds has, at its center,

$$
\mathrm{CNR}_{\text{wall}} = \frac{C}{\sigma_n}\operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{w}{2\sqrt2\,\sigma}\right), \qquad
w_{\min} = 2\sqrt2\,\sigma\,\operatorname{erf}^{-1}\!\left(\frac{k\,\sigma_n}{C}\right)
$$ {#eq-m48-visibility}

where $w_{\min}$ is the thinnest wall that reaches a chosen CNR $k$ (it exists only if $k\sigma_n < C$). With
$C/\sigma_n = 5$, 1 mm of blur and an illustrative $k = 3$, $w_{\min}$ = 0.71 mm. In lab part E, smoothing the mean
wall from 0.25 to 2 mm raises its CNR from 4.2 to 12.5 (illustrative noise), but from 1.5 mm on the wall merges with
an esophageal wall 2 mm away, and the esophagus spills 8% of its signal into the wall's center.

**Key takeaways**

- CNR, not contrast alone, decides visibility; averaging gains $\sqrt n$.
- Smoothing trades noise for resolution; there is no free lunch across a structure.

### Accuracy of an imaging test

Sensitivity (Se) and specificity (Sp) describe the test; predictive values describe what a result means in a
population with prevalence $\pi$ ([eq-m35-ppv](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-ppv)). Likelihood ratios separate the
two:

$$
\mathrm{LR}^+ = \frac{\mathrm{Se}}{1 - \mathrm{Sp}}, \qquad \mathrm{LR}^- = \frac{1 - \mathrm{Se}}{\mathrm{Sp}},
\qquad \frac{p_{\text{post}}}{1 - p_{\text{post}}} = \frac{\pi}{1 - \pi}\,\mathrm{LR}
$$ {#eq-m48-lr}

where $p_{\text{post}}$ is the probability of disease after the result; with $\mathrm{LR}^+$ it equals the PPV, and
with $\mathrm{LR}^-$ it equals one minus the NPV. For CT and appendage thrombus [@romero2013], $\mathrm{LR}^+$ = 12
and $\mathrm{LR}^-$ = 0.043. At 8.9% prevalence the formula gives a PPV of 54% and an NPV of 99.6%; the meta-analysis
reported pooled values of 41% and 99%. They need not agree, because each measure was pooled across studies
separately and PPV depends on each study's prevalence. PPV is concave in prevalence, so the average of per-study PPVs
lies below the PPV at the average prevalence (lab part G shows this on illustrative studies); that is one possible
reason, not a full account. With delayed imaging (Se 100%, Sp 99%) the formula gives 91%, against 92% reported.

::: {.demo #m48-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m48-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m48-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m48-d2-predictive-values.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: [eq-m35-ppv](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-ppv) and @eq-m48-lr, with sensitivity and specificity that do
  not change with prevalence. Tested against `epml.overview` and `epml.ml`.
- Presets and reported pooled values: CT against TEE for appendage thrombus, 19 studies and 2,955 patients
  [@romero2013].
- What it ignores: uncertainty in the pooled estimates, differences between studies, and the imperfection of TEE as
  the reference standard.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Sensitivity and specificity belong to the test; predictive values belong to the test in a population.
- Pooled predictive values from a meta-analysis are not the formula applied to pooled sensitivity and specificity.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where this shows up in EP.** Patients with AF may have imaging before, during and after ablation. The EACVI/EHRA
expert consensus reviews echocardiography (left atrial volume and strain), MRI (left atrial fibrosis), CT (with
emphasis on planning interventions) and nuclear imaging in these patients, and reaches fourteen consensus statements
meant to help imagers and electrophysiologists choose and interpret the technique [@donal2016].

**What the evidence is.** A 2016 expert consensus [@donal2016], and, for the worked example, one meta-analysis of
diagnostic accuracy with TEE as the reference [@romero2013]. The table of questions above mixes randomized trials,
registries, cohorts and consensus; each module m49–m55 discusses its own evidence. Newer studies may have changed
what the consensus describes; it is read here for its structure, not as current advice.

**What a reader should ask:**

- **Which question is the image meant to answer?** The modality follows from it.
- **At what resolution and contrast?** A thin structure or a small difference may be below what the image can show
  (@eq-m48-psf, @eq-m48-visibility).
- **In which population?** Predictive values move with prevalence (@eq-m48-lr).

## How experts think

Before choosing or trusting an image, ask:

1. **What is the question?** Anatomy, wall, scar, thrombus, inflammation, catheter position or dose.
2. **Can this modality resolve it?** Compare the structure's size with the FWHM (@eq-m48-psf).
3. **Is there contrast, and enough CNR?** Which agent or sequence creates the difference, and how noisy is it
   (@eq-m48-cnr, @eq-m48-visibility)?
4. **What did processing do?** Smoothing and thresholds change what is seen and measured (@eq-m48-smooth).
5. **What does a result mean here?** Use the prevalence in this population, not the one in the paper (@eq-m48-lr).

One sentence to keep: **an image answers a question at a resolution, a contrast and a prevalence; change any one and
the answer changes.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| PSF and FWHM (@eq-m48-psf) | $\Gamma = 2\sqrt{2\ln 2}\,\sigma \approx 2.355\,\sigma$; two points show a dip only if $d > 2\sigma$ |
| Thin wall ([eq-m51-wall](m51-cardiac-ct.qmd#eq-m51-wall)) | Peak $\operatorname{erf}(w/(2\sqrt2\,\sigma))$; FWHM reading never below $\Gamma$ |
| CNR (@eq-m48-cnr) | $\lvert S_A - S_B\rvert/\sigma_n$; averaging $n$ samples gains $\sqrt n$; dose ×4 halves photon noise |
| Smoothing (@eq-m48-smooth) | 2-D white noise falls to $\sigma_n\Delta/(2\sqrt\pi\,\sigma_s)$; blur adds in quadrature |
| Wall visibility (@eq-m48-visibility) | $\mathrm{CNR}_{\text{wall}} = (C/\sigma_n)\operatorname{erf}(w/(2\sqrt2\,\sigma))$ |
| Likelihood ratios (@eq-m48-lr) | $\mathrm{LR}^+ = \mathrm{Se}/(1-\mathrm{Sp})$; post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR |

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. What is the FWHM of a Gaussian blur, and why use it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The distance between the points where the PSF falls to half its peak,
$2\sqrt{2\ln 2}\,\sigma \approx 2.355\,\sigma$ (@eq-m48-psf). It is easy to measure on a line or point phantom and roughly the separation at which two structures
start to merge.

</details>

**Q2. When do two blurred points show a dip between them?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

When their separation exceeds $2\sigma$, about 0.85 FWHM: the curvature of the sum at the midpoint is proportional
to $d^2/4 - \sigma^2$ (@eq-m48-psf). At one FWHM the dip is only about 7%, so with noise they may still look like one.

</details>

**Q3. A 0.5-mm wall imaged at 1.5 mm FWHM. What do you expect?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Its peak reaches about 31% of its contrast ([eq-m51-wall](m51-cardiac-ct.qmd#eq-m51-wall)); a half-contrast
threshold misses it, and a half-peak reading reports about 1.5 mm, the blur, not the wall.

</details>

**Q4. Why do blood and myocardium look almost the same on fluoroscopy and non-contrast CT?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Their X-ray attenuation is nearly equal: at 60 keV they differ by about 5 HU, and 2 mm of wall against blood
changes a projection by about 0.02% (lab part C). Iodine in the blood creates the difference.

</details>

**Q5. Define CNR. How does it change with averaging and with dose?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$|S_A - S_B|/\sigma_n$ (@eq-m48-cnr). Averaging $n$ independent samples multiplies it by $\sqrt n$. For
photon-limited noise, CNR grows with the square root of the dose, so doubling CNR costs four times the dose
([eq-m49-cnr](m49-fluoroscopy-radiation.qmd#eq-m49-cnr)).

</details>

**Q6. What does smoothing do to noise and resolution?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

In 2-D it divides white noise by $2\sqrt\pi\,\sigma_s/\Delta$ and widens the blur to
$\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \sigma_s^2}$ (@eq-m48-smooth). A wall's CNR rises, but neighbors merge and spill into it (lab part E).

</details>

**Q7. How thin a wall can you see?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Pick a CNR you need, $k$. Then
$w_{\min} = 2\sqrt2\,\sigma\,\operatorname{erf}^{-1}(k\sigma_n/C)$ (@eq-m48-visibility), and no wall is visible if $k\sigma_n \ge C$. Better contrast or less noise lowers it, as does a
smaller $\sigma$.

</details>

**Q8. Sensitivity 96%, specificity 92%, prevalence 8.9%. What is the PPV?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

About 54% ([eq-m35-ppv](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-ppv)). Equivalently, LR+ = 12, pre-test odds 0.098, post-test
odds 1.17 (@eq-m48-lr).

</details>

**Q9. A meta-analysis reports pooled sensitivity, specificity and PPV that do not satisfy Bayes' rule. Is it wrong?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Not necessarily. Each measure is pooled across studies separately, and PPV depends on each study's prevalence; since
PPV is concave in prevalence, averaging per-study PPVs gives less than the PPV at the average prevalence. For CT and
appendage thrombus the formula gives 54% against a reported 41% [@romero2013].

</details>

**Q10. Why are likelihood ratios useful for imaging tests?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

They summarize the test independently of prevalence and update any pre-test probability by multiplying
odds (@eq-m48-lr). A high LR+ rules in, a low LR− rules out.

</details>

**Q11. How would you compare two modalities for measuring atrial wall thickness?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

By resolution against the thickness range (0.5–3.5 mm [@beinart2011]), wall contrast against blood and fat, noise
and reading method (threshold or half-peak), against a reference such as histology or a phantom of known thickness.
Report bias as a function of thickness, not one mean error.

</details>

**Q12. Why is PET poor at showing wall thickness but still useful in EP?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Its 4–7 mm resolution [@kinahan2010] is coarser than the wall, so thickness is lost and uptake is underestimated by
partial volume (m54). It answers a different question: where a tracer accumulates, for example inflammation or
infection [@muser2018; @bourque2024].

</details>

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. A PSF has σ = 1 mm. FWHM?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

About 2.4 mm (@eq-m48-psf).

</details>

**S2. With that PSF, how close can two points be and still show a dip?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Just over 2 mm (@eq-m48-psf).

</details>

**S3. CNR is 2 per pixel. Average 9 independent pixels. CNR?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

6 (@eq-m48-cnr).

</details>

**S4. Smoothing σ_s doubles. What happens to 2-D white noise?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

It halves (@eq-m48-smooth).

</details>

**S5. Se 100%, Sp 99%. LR+?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

100 (@eq-m48-lr).

**S6. True or false: a test's PPV is a property of the scanner.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

False: it depends on prevalence ([eq-m35-ppv](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-ppv)).

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Measured resolution of a CT system.** Rajendran et al. show modulation transfer functions and section
  sensitivity profiles for standard and high-resolution modes [@rajendran2022;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8940675/)]. This module: blur and resolution.
- **Resolution and SUV in PET.** Kinahan and Fletcher discuss how resolution and partial volume affect measured
  uptake [@kinahan2010; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3026294/)]. This module: thin walls.

## Further reading

- **Imaging in AF.** EACVI/EHRA expert consensus [@donal2016].
- **Diagnostic accuracy.** CT for appendage thrombus [@romero2013]; predictive values and Bayes' rule
  [@altman1994].
- **Resolution in practice.** Photon-counting CT [@rajendran2022]; LGE [@kellman2012]; PET [@kinahan2010].
- **Related modules.** m35 for diagnostic accuracy, m49 for fluoroscopy, m50 for ICE, m51 for CT, m52 and m53 for MRI,
  m54 for nuclear imaging, and m55 for putting them together.
